episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

D.J. Paris sits down with Kevin McCarthy, cofounder of Real Geeks, who has built real estate agent websites for 20 years. They cover how ChatGPT and Claude decide which agents to recommend, why a website and local content matter again, and how Real Geeks’ new AI Connect lets agents create and update pages just by asking.

What you’ll learn

  • You need a website with real content. Kevin says AI answers come from two places: what the model learned in training, and a live search it runs when someone asks. To show up in either, have a site that covers you, your services and your neighborhoods, and that ranks well on Google. (08:44)
  • AI bots are already a big share of site traffic. On the websites Kevin’s company runs, he says about 40% of traffic is AI agents, mostly crawlers reading every page. (10:13)
  • Your social posts don’t help you get found by AI. Kevin says OpenAI can’t crawl Instagram, so content that lives only on social isn’t visible to answer engines. (14:59)
  • Publish what nobody else has. Pick a topic where you hold knowledge that isn’t anywhere else on the internet, such as a new building in your area. (23:32)
  • AI-written content is fine if it is useful. Kevin says Google’s position is that AI content is fine as long as it is good, so research first and don’t copy and paste raw output. (42:30)

“…find something where it’s just about you and especially something where you have knowledge that nobody else on the internet has.”

Kevin McCarthy (at 23:32)

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

In this monthly Breakthrough with Michael session, performance coach Michael Opyd coaches Mengjiao “MJ” Chen live. MJ is a former special education teacher and Mandarin interpreter who went full time in real estate in the greater Seattle area, with a focus on Bellevue. She books appointments from cold calls, then stalls on follow-up, and the conversation is about building a system that fits how she works.

What you’ll learn

  • Cold calls to expired listings can book appointments. MJ says she can book one appointment a day by calling expired listings and offering to help the owner find out why the house did not sell. (11:13)
  • Call reluctance is normal. MJ admits she sometimes drifts from strangers to friends on her call list, and D.J. says he would do the same. (19:35)
  • The sticking point is what happens after the call. MJ is avoiding sending a net sheet because she does not know what comes next, and she has no repeatable follow-up after open houses. (14:48)
  • A copied system is not the goal. MJ hoped to read a book or find a system she could duplicate. Michael answers that the quicker you build a business that fits who you are, the easier everything else gets. (42:20)
  • Sort your friction into good and bad. Bad friction comes from a piece of the business that does not fit you. Good friction comes from growth in something you are good at. (51:34)

“I feel like I am a person need a very clear direction breakdown step by step. If you said call those 20 people, I have no problem pick up the phone to call the 20 people.”

Mengjiao Chen (at 14:48)

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

D.J. Paris sits down with Nick Schlekeway, founder and managing broker of Amherst Madison Real Estate Advisors in Boise, Idaho, and author of The Essential Agent. They cover why he manages energy instead of time, the four pillars top producers build their days around, how he nearly quit after 30 offers went nowhere, and the simple outreach system he used to stay in touch with his sphere.

What you’ll learn

  • Manage your energy, not your clock. Time blocking works until the phone blows up in the late morning. Nick prioritizes his day around energy instead. (07:06)
  • Prospect first, right after you take care of yourself. Prospect generation takes the most energy, so it goes right after mind, body and spirit, not in the afternoon. (10:10)
  • Focus means saying no. The market rewards specificity, and agents move to the next level when they declare what they will be known for. (17:14)
  • Use the 411 to stay in touch. Four phone calls a year, one mailing a month and one digital contact a week, which Nick says can cover a sphere of up to 300 people. (45:54)
  • Ask for the referral before closing. Clients are still thinking about real estate then, and Nick suggests staying high touch for the weeks before and after closing. (49:57)

“…prospect generation is about the will and conversion is a skill.”

Nick Schlekeway (at 41:34)

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

In this YouTube Lab episode, Sarah Maslowski of Keypoint Homes Group, who serves buyers in North Georgia, shows how one YouTube video can be found through YouTube, Google and AI tools. She explains how to turn a video script into a search-friendly blog post, link related articles together and keep them current.

What you’ll learn

  • Google owns YouTube, so video can show up in search. Sarah points out that search results now include videos and AI-generated answers, which gives a video another way to be found. (05:00)
  • Make content around the questions people ask. Buyers search cost of living, property taxes and where to live before they ever look for an agent. (06:38)
  • No trick guarantees an AI recommendation. Some AI tools can search the public web and cite sources, so helpful original content gives them more to work with. (12:21)
  • Turn your script into a blog post. Paste your YouTube script into an AI tool, ask it to use only your information, then check the facts and edit it into short paragraphs. (16:22)
  • Link your articles to each other and keep them current. Related posts should point to one another, and topics like mortgage rates and property taxes need updating. (22:45)

“We are creating content around questions. People are already asking.”

Sarah Maslowski (at 06:59)

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

D.J. Paris sits down with Kate Ziegler Romano, co-owner of New Englander Real Estate in the Boston area, who also manages and renovates a rental portfolio with her husband. They cover what she does for clients in the first 90 days after closing, how she builds a trusted list of contractors, and how owning rental property steadies her income in slow years.

What you’ll learn

  • Send seasonal home tips, not just holiday cards. Kate reminds past clients to shut off outside spigots, drain water lines or service the air conditioner, which keeps her name in front of them and helps first-time buyers who don’t know these things. (06:58)
  • Text early and don’t fear what’s broken. She checks in at one week and one month after closing. Something is always wrong with a house, and clients who hear from you commiserate instead of blaming you. (40:53)
  • Keep the outreach personal. Kate texts clients when she drives by or sees something that reminds her of them, and keeps going even when they don’t answer. Most of her business comes from those relationships. (43:01)
  • Build your vendor list from your clients’ experience. If you don’t hire trades yourself, ask clients who they used and whether they liked them, then drop anyone who isn’t showing up. (50:21)
  • Use rental income to smooth out quiet years. Owning rental units means she isn’t panicking about the next closing. (38:29)

“They won’t blame you if you’re not ghosting them, if you’re not totally gone. They feel like you’re still on their team.”

Kate Ziegler Romano (at 41:55)

D.J. Paris sits down with Justin Helmus, a top 1% producer in Tampa Bay and an NAR 30 Under 30 honoree who has sold the highest-priced condo on Clearwater Beach and the highest-priced home in Belleair for their years. They cover why he ignored the advice to let business come to him, how he wins luxury and investor clients, and the plan he would follow in a first 12 months.

What you’ll learn

  • Know the market better than anyone. At 25, Justin knew he couldn’t out-relationship agents with decades in town, so he learned every segment of the market and every detail of a property. (05:57)
  • Handwritten notes beat more social posts. He writes and hand delivers notes to prospective buyers and other luxury agents, and looks ahead at life events like a graduation. (13:54)
  • Go where your ideal clients are. He sat at the table nearest the door of a copy shop with old MLS sheets, and says it led to five to 10 deals. (29:04)
  • Build a team around a target listing. For a home he wants, he sends a handwritten note, then asks a neighbor and a mutual friend to put in a good word. (32:00)
  • Study the market every day. Justin spends at least an hour a day on what’s going on, because if he doesn’t, his competition is. (26:38)

“I mean, handwritten notes, bar none, is the best use of your time, in my opinion.”

Justin Helmus (at 14:35)

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

Live from Zillow Unlock 2026 in Las Vegas, D.J. Paris sits down with Mischa Fisher, Chief Economist at Zillow. They cover why some markets are rising while others cool, the one number agents should check every month, how to talk to buyers about today’s rates, and what to plan for before spring 2027.

What you’ll learn

  • Check one number a month. Mischa’s pick is the change in Zillow’s home values, because it shows the balance of supply and demand better than sold prices or price cuts. Right now home values are rising, but by less than inflation. (10:53)
  • Buyers have more choice than they’ve had in years. Inventory has grown for more than 30 months in a row in most markets. (16:14)
  • Pricing is where listings are won or lost. Well-priced listings with full exposure are selling in the normal amount of time. Get the strategy wrong and the listing lingers. (24:13)
  • Watch your local rental market. The gap between renting and owning has been shrinking, and as it shrinks, more renters turn into buyers. (29:54)
  • Get ready for volatility. If rates drop faster than expected, competition ramps up quickly. Reconnect with your sphere now, not when it happens. (31:15)

“If you’re getting that listing strategy wrong, then you’re looking at lingering for months and you’re in the price cut purgatory.”

Mischa Fisher (at 24:17)

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

Kim Rittberg, a speaking and video coach for real estate agents and founders, and a former TV producer and media executive who worked at Netflix, joins Keeping It Real for a short solo episode on AI. She explains why generic AI content makes agents look the same, and how to use AI and video to show clients who you are.

What you’ll learn

  • AI exposes generic content. If your posts are something anyone with an AI account could make, or just what your brokerage hands you, they won’t help clients get to know or trust you. (04:21)
  • Tell AI about yourself. Give it your audience, your area and what sets you apart, such as a finance background, a love of interior design or strong negotiating, so the scripts are for you and not for anybody. (05:39)
  • Redline the draft like a contract. Change anything that doesn’t sound like you or doesn’t show you as the expert, and skip any script another agent in your area could also make. (06:36)
  • Win the first two seconds. Every video needs a compelling opening, because that moment either sinks the content or makes it work. (07:45)
  • Your speaking skills set you apart. Because everyone else is making the same kind of content, showing up on video makes you more competitive and more compelling. (08:51)

“So the one thing that AI cannot copy right now is you. You being uniquely charming, you being uniquely insightful, you having decades of experience, maybe one year, maybe 20 years of experience, that is what AI can’t copy.”

Kim Rittberg (at 05:15)

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

Sarah Maslowski, a real estate agent who says she has closed over $140 million in real estate directly from YouTube with no paid ads and no cold calling, hosts this solo episode of The YouTube Lab on Keeping It Real. She takes on the fear that stops most agents before they press record, and answers the most common excuses one by one.

What you’ll learn

  • Successful channels aren’t polished. The agents getting leads and closings from YouTube were regular agents talking about life in their area, not TV hosts. Sarah realized she only had to show up as herself and give people the information they were looking for. (04:34)
  • Editing hides the stumbles. You can stop, fumble a sentence and start again while filming, and a good editor leaves one clean, confident thought. (05:59)
  • Comfort comes from doing it. Sarah says nobody is comfortable on camera at first. A teleprompter app can take the pressure off if going off the cuff feels terrifying. (06:49)
  • Your market is your content. The best neighborhoods, the commute and what surprises people about moving there are questions you have answered for clients for years. (08:28)
  • There is room for you. Even with a dozen agents making videos about her market, Sarah says they are all getting business, and that YouTube produces the most leads of the platforms agents use. (09:02)

“Nobody is comfortable on camera at first. Nobody. Comfort comes from doing it, not from waiting until you feel ready.”

Sarah Maslowski (at 06:49)

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

D.J. Paris sits down with Anna Kara, a loan officer who started as a receptionist and built her own mortgage company by age 20, and who works with borrowers in all 50 states. They cover how to talk to buyers who want to wait for lower rates, why the monthly payment matters more than the rate, how she helps self-employed borrowers, and how to build a brand people remember.

What you’ll learn

  • Waiting for lower rates creates competition. Anna says a house with five competing buyers today can draw 20 or 30 when rates drop, and she has seen 61 offers on one transaction. The rate can change later, but the purchase price can’t. (21:54)
  • Show the payment, not just the rate. When she locks a rate she gives buyers six or seven options with costs and payments side by side, so they can see when paying $12,000 up front doesn’t make sense. (17:38)
  • Self-employed borrowers are often turned down because of the filing. Anna works with the borrower’s CPA so allowable add-backs aren’t lost, and she has bank statement and asset depletion programs when tax returns aren’t enough. (09:25)
  • Say “here’s the reality,” not “I’ll fix this.” After a deal stalled for weeks while a borrower’s accounts were shut down, Anna changed how she talks to clients: lay out the situation and what she can do, then let them decide. (35:34)
  • Build your brand on being real. Anna gives information and never pitches. She says people remember the person they feel they know when they are ready to buy, and that authenticity and consistency matter most. (26:48)

“And if they make sense, they make sense. Numbers don’t lie at the end of the day.”

Anna Kara (at 14:42)

  • Do the scary thing, then leave people behind. Each time you do something that scares you, like picking up the phone, you pass the agents who didn’t. Ben says he has trained himself to get excited when something scares him. (08:50)
  • Run an autopsy on your past deals. List where each transaction came from, then ask why that person referred you and what triggered it. Pick the activities you can repeat, not the lucky ones, and do those for the next 90 days. (13:40)

In this Monday Market Minute, D.J. Paris sits down with Carrie McCormick, who leads the Carrie McCormick Luxury Group at @properties Christie’s International Real Estate in Chicago. They cover how to answer “how’s the market?”, what luxury buyers want right now, how to price a listing this fall, and how clients are using AI to challenge agents.

What you’ll learn

  • Answer “how’s the market?” with a question. Each neighborhood, building, housing stock and price point performs differently, so Carrie asks which market and which segment the person means. She says that specific answer builds credibility. (07:35)
  • Luxury buyers are discerning. Carrie lists location, architecture, privacy, views, land, condition and a home that feels special as what matters to buyers around $5 million. Most want plug and play, because time is their most valuable resource. (09:29)
  • Don’t chase the market this fall. The first few weeks on the market are when everyone is watching, so Carrie says to watch pricing, activity and marketing in the first two weeks. Pricing, presentation and positioning matter most. (14:43)
  • AI is a fact-checker, not a replacement. Clients now arrive saying “my chat said this,” so Carrie says agents have to know their information cold. She uses AI as a coach and always double checks it. (18:44)
  • Be there when they decide. Carrie stays away from automated touch points because she wants the human touch, and she uses a Nordstrom shoe department story to explain why: you want to be the person standing there when the client is ready. (29:24)

“If the house is sitting on the market more than 120 days, they see that as a negotiating strategy. So the buyers have become so intuitive into what this market is.”

  • Use AI to make local history content. He photographed a book about Cape Coral, had Claude turn it into video ideas and colorized old photos, and the videos drew more than 100,000 views. (1:01:44)

Paris sits down with Bill Melnick, a luxury agent with Harney Real Estate in Litchfield County, Connecticut, who spent 28 years at Ralph Lauren and rose to chief merchandising officer before switching careers. They cover how a lifestyle-merchandising mindset shapes his listings, how he sold Ivan Lendl’s estate for a county-record $12 million, and why second-primary buyers are changing his market.

What you’ll learn

  • Sell the lifestyle, not just the house. Bill says luxury buyers look for 360 degrees of lifestyle: the location, the cachet, the home and the view. His job is to present all of it in a cohesive way. (05:58)
  • Edit before you photograph. Staging is mostly editing. Remove clutter and anything that becomes visual pollution so buyers can picture their own things in the space. (07:34)
  • Price is more than square footage. In his market, lakefront, big mountain views and pools can add real money, and so can usable acreage and conservation land next door. Bill calls it a much more complicated equation. (11:36)
  • At the top end, you find the buyer. On the Lendl estate, Bill partnered with his broker and called top agents in nearby markets and New York City. He says a lot of agents don’t understand that in luxury you often have to find the buyer for the listing. (19:43)
  • Go easy on AI for client messages. Bill uses AI for research and for drafting brochure copy that he edits, but he says answering every email with it is a turn-off for buyers and other agents. (42:07)

“…a lot of agents don’t understand about luxury is a lot of times you got to find the buyer for the listing agent.”

Paris sits down with Alex Maldonado, a Los Angeles agent with Circle Real Estate who serves South LA, East LA, Northeast LA and Long Beach, works with first-time and first-generation buyers in English and Spanish, and also runs Maldonado Marketing. They cover how to close the gap when a buyer has the down payment but not the closing costs, how to keep an offer with credits competitive, and how Alex generates leads.

What you’ll learn

  • Cover closing costs with credits. Alex works with a lender who offers lender credits and writes seller credits into the contract. If the buyer has the 3.5% down payment, or can get it from family, he says he can usually get them to ownership. (08:26)
  • Make the offer strong in other ways. To offset credits, Alex builds them into the price, offers 3% earnest money and uses a lender that can close in 21 days, because sellers care about their net and speed. (15:53)
  • Break bad news slowly. When a buyer fell in love with a neighborhood she couldn’t afford, Alex sent her recent closing prices so she could judge for herself, and explained that many of the listings were cash-only. (13:41)
  • Know your local assistance programs. Alex explains city and county down payment assistance as a way to get in the door and start building wealth, in exchange for giving up a share of the appreciation. (19:10)
  • Earn trust in the Hispanic community. Alex says referrals carry the most weight, and a client invited him to speak at her church after he told her to walk away from a property with termite and foundation problems. (28:59)

“…I first get to the root cause of it because everyone has a different motivation for wanting to be a homeowner.”

In this month’s Unpopular Real Estate Opinions, D.J. Paris sits down with Chris Linsell, Chief Marketing Officer at the Mitten Group, a Michigan brokerage group based in Traverse City. They cover how AI will split the agent profession in two, why organic social is out-converting paid leads for his brokerage, and what Zillow and Compass mean for independent brokerages.

What you’ll learn

  • AI rewards relationship builders. Chris says agents whose value is relationships and advice get a “miracle technology,” because the back-end admin work goes away and they can spend their time on clients. (14:49)
  • Lock box value is at risk. Chris predicts that agents whose main value is operating a lock box and confirming showings could be reclassified as gig workers within 18 to 24 months, while top agents hire them for the grunt work. (16:31)
  • Disruption opens business up. Chris argues that if the weakest-performing agents drop out, a share of transactions becomes unassigned, and doing nothing is the one guaranteed way not to reach your goals. (23:53)
  • Organic social beats paid leads on conversion. At the Mitten Group, Chris says organic social is now a more important lead source than paid, because the conversion rates and relationships from opt-in followers are not comparable. (27:06)
  • Watch independent brokerages and Zillow. Chris expects Zillow to keep growing and says some independent brokerages may start quietly planning exits from Zillow-related obligations, with strong storytellers explaining why the independent model is better. (33:49)

“…if you are a real estate agent who has no value outside of your ability to operate a lock box, my prediction is that in the next 18 to 24 months, you will be reclassified as a gig worker in this space.”

  • Build a reserve before you spend on marketing. She sets 20% aside for taxes, pays her bills, then builds a reserve that covers four months of expenses. (53:03)

“We are in a people business and you don’t get in front of people by just sitting around.”

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

D.J. Paris sits down with Chris Wands, founder of the Wands Team at Douglas Elliman in Miami. They cover how rentals launched his career, why his team ranks number four nationally for rental transactions, how he advises buyers on condo risk, and how he stays in touch with clients after the sale.

What you’ll learn

  • Treat every rental as a future transaction. Chris calls real estate a contact sport: owners, tenants and other brokers all see your name on the deal, and you never know where that door opens. (16:44)
  • Rentals can be a real business line. His team did 71 rentals in the first six months of the year, which he puts at over $220,000 in GCI from rentals alone. (29:22)
  • Give buyers the facts on condos. His transaction coordinator pulls the condo documents as soon as an offer comes in, and he lets clients decide on special assessments based on their own risk tolerance. (35:04)
  • Be the advisor, even when it costs a sale. If a buyer has nothing to buy yet, Chris will suggest a rental instead, and clients at that level can tell when you are not being genuine. (39:43)
  • Build the infrastructure before you scale. He waited on a larger team until he had admin staff, a marketing director and a system in place. (43:22)

“So the way I looked at it with rentals is it’s a contact sport. Every single time you meet someone, it’s not whether or not you close that transaction. It’s the future transaction.”

D.J. Paris sits down with Vija Williams, who leads a team of residential agents in the Seattle and Puget Sound market and works with Realty.com on cash offer seller leads. They cover how sellers now research with AI and online estimates before they ever call an agent, and what that means for the way agents show up.

What you’ll learn

  • The agent is now the last opinion. Sellers used to call an agent first. Now they check an estimate, ask an AI chatbot or request a cash offer before an agent comes in to explain what it all means. (17:33)
  • Get in before they pick an agent. Vija says most sellers still hire the first agent they meet, so the goal is to reach them while they are still researching. (22:01)
  • Put valuations and tracking on your site. Home valuations, a home report you can see them open, and a CRM that flags changing behavior show you who is moving toward selling. (22:50)
  • A cash offer is one option, not the whole plan. Vija says only about one in 20 of these leads ends in a cash sale, and that the rest are listing leads. (28:09)
  • Think in a pyramid of intent. At the top are home valuation leads, who may only be curious, and at the bottom are people who want a cash offer now. (30:04)

“…the real estate agent started off as the first phone call. We are now the last opinion.”

In this YouTube Lab episode, Sarah Maslowski of Keypoint Homes Group in Georgia shares how she thinks about titles and thumbnails. She says she has closed over $150 million in real estate from YouTube with no paid ads and no cold calling, and she walks through the title mistakes agents make, how to research better titles and her full thumbnail system.

What you’ll learn

  • A title has one job. It is not to describe the video. It is to make someone curious enough to click. (04:30)
  • Use AI for title ideas. Drop your first title into an AI tool and ask for 10 more clickable versions, then narrow it to two or three. (07:04)
  • Let YouTube test it. The built-in A/B test shows which title or thumbnail viewers actually click, so you stop guessing. (07:31)
  • Treat the thumbnail like a magazine cover. Use a big face with a real expression, a background that shows the topic, consistent fonts and colors, and no more than three to five words. (09:05)
  • Keep the editor and thumbnail designer separate. The skills are different, and in her experience thumbnails from video editors have underperformed. (15:14)

“Titles and thumbnails are the front door of your YouTube channel.”

In this month’s Learning With A Lender episode, D.J. Paris talks with Austin Clarence, a mortgage loan officer and investor financing specialist at Nexa Mortgage. They cover how oil prices and the Fed feed into mortgage rates, why home values have kept rising, and loan programs agents can bring to doctors, veterans and self-employed buyers.

What you’ll learn

  • Oil prices reach mortgage rates. Oil touches trucking, shipping and manufacturing, so it shows up in inflation. With crude down from about $120 to $69 a barrel, Austin expects relief to reach rates over the coming months. (06:53)
  • Home values kept rising. Even with elevated rates, Austin points to national appreciation, which is a good talking point for buyers deciding whether to wait. (15:25)
  • Ask buyers what they do for work. Doctor loans can mean no down payment and no PMI, and they can be more forgiving of student loans. (21:07)
  • VA loans are easier to qualify for. He says FHA loans max out at a 56% debt-to-income ratio at every lender, while a VA loan can go up to 70% with residual income. (26:48)
  • Self-employed buyers have options. An FHA program with 3.5% down lets buyers prepare their own profit and loss statement instead of waiting on tax returns. (32:28)

“Oil is really involved with everything with trucking, shipping, manufacturing. It’s not just filling up at the pump. It’s everything that gets to the grocery store, everything that you’re purchasing online, the Amazon driver.”

  • Never skip the buyer consult. Sarah says her most painful clients almost always trace back to a skipped or rushed consult. (19:15)

“Relocation buyers are making a massive emotional decision. They need to trust you before they’ll follow your guidance.”

  • Don’t forget older buyers. Homeowners with equity who are downsizing or facing a life event are an overlooked group that needs an agent’s help. (43:09)

They cover how she prepares sellers before listing, how she uses facts and data to talk about price, what she does to stay in touch, and why her business runs on referrals.

What you’ll learn

  • Have the hard conversation. Natalie’s HR background shapes how she talks plainly with sellers. If she only tells them what they want to hear, nobody wins. (06:31)
  • Bring solutions, not just recommendations. She tells sellers what needs to be done, then offers her network of people to do it before the home goes to market. (08:00)
  • Let the data set the price. Natalie walks sellers through comps slide by slide, so the price comes from the market and not from her opinion. (09:47)
  • Keep touching listings that haven’t sold. She updates sellers on what has gone under contract and closed since they listed, and on why those homes were picked over theirs. (20:29)
  • Build referrals through community. Her involvement with the local Humane Society led a for-sale-by-owner seller to call her. (11:15)
  • Give clients something tangible. She hands buyers a binder with the marketing and transaction details, so they remember her when they think of the house. (31:56)

“No one wants to talk about the hard stuff, but you have to. And I always tell people, if I just go into a listing and I just tell them what they want to hear, no one wins in that situation.”

In this Better Your Business With Ben episode, D.J. Paris talks with Ben Lalez, who leads the Ben Lalez Team in Chicago and hangs his license with Compass. They sort out the Zillow, Compass and MLS fight over private listings, then turn to how Ben uses AI to cut expenses, build an offer-guarantee product and create content.

What you’ll learn

  • Nobody in the listing fight speaks for the agent. Ben says Zillow and Compass each claim to serve the consumer, while both answer to shareholders. He wants agents to plant their flag in their own yard. (13:02)
  • Connect your own data to an AI tool and let it ask you questions. Ben synced his transaction and bank data and built a real-time view of income and expenses, and says he reduced his monthly spend on people by about five grand a month. (31:11)
  • Your deal history can predict cancellations. Ben’s five years of transactions showed about 17% of his contracts died, and the source of the lead, earnest money and contract terms all moved the odds. (37:50)
  • That analysis became OfferShield. Ben’s team promises a seller a payout if the buyer cancels. He says they have issued 12 policies so far. (41:45)
  • Start small with a scheduled task. Ben suggests having Claude run an overnight task on something your area cares about, like restaurant openings, then build from there. (58:18)

“So every problem that us real estate agents are having, there is a creative solution. There are novel solutions to these problems.”

In this Inner Game of Real Estate Success episode, high-performance hypnotherapist and mindset coach Paul Salter explains why busy agents drift off track as their business grows. Using a GPS metaphor, he argues the way back is to return to the routines and boundaries that made you effective, not to work harder, and he walks through a calendar audit to start.

What you’ll learn

  • The habits that build your business can wear you down later. Being always available gets rewarded early, but over time Paul says you end up running below your capacity and never switching off. (03:36)
  • “Once things slow down” never arrives. Paul says the real issue is not workload but that you drifted from the routines and fundamentals that kept you grounded. (05:18)
  • Do what a GPS does: recalculate and return to the route. When you feel off track, speeding up and taking random turns makes it worse. (07:19)
  • Intensity needs rest. Paul compares agents to an Olympic sprinter, who trains through planned periods of high intensity and planned periods of rest. (13:46)
  • Audit your calendar. Put workouts, date nights and family time on it first, then build your work around them. (21:01)

“…you don’t need another productivity hack. You don’t need another AI bot. You don’t need more motivation. You need to return to the fundamentals that made you effective before success made you reactive.”

  • Write a voice guide for your AI. Keep your content from sounding like generic output by giving AI tools your own editorial standards. (49:14)

“…we do not as real estate agents identify our value based on the brokerage logo on our signs our value gets identified by the agent name on the rider on top of the sign…”

In this YouTube Lab episode, host Sarah Maslowski interviews Gino D’Angelo, a Northern Michigan agent and coach who works a high-end resort market. Gino explains why he moved from paying for Zillow leads to building his business on YouTube, what his first 90 days looked like, and why a small market can be an advantage.

  • He stopped renting leads. Gino says he was spending about $8,000 a month on Zillow leads and got tired of being treated like an Uber driver, so he tried YouTube. (04:23)
  • Expect a slow drip at first. About 90 days in, the videos started producing business, and now it is a big part of his business. (05:13)
  • Start cheap. Gino says he paid too much for a videographer early on, and that he would keep costs as low as possible until the videos make money. (12:41)
  • One hour a week keeps paying. He records in a studio room in his office, hands the video to an editor, and says videos from two years ago still bring in leads. (16:13)
  • Viewers arrive ready to hire you. By the time someone calls after watching your videos, Gino says they already feel they know you. (17:15)
  • Make videos for people moving to your area. A video about one park is too narrow, so Sarah suggests putting that kind of detail inside a larger “living here” video. (32:04)
  • Build a runway. Film a few videos ahead so life does not interrupt your weekly posting. (36:07)

“…we shouldn’t be expecting tens of thousands of views on our videos we just need the right people watching our content.”

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

In this Learning With A Lender episode, D.J. Paris talks with Austin Clarence, a mortgage loan officer and investor financing specialist with Nexa Mortgage. They cover the Federal Reserve chair change and what it means for mortgage rates, how DSCR loans work for investors, where to find investor clients, and how buydowns can help buyers in today’s rate environment.

What you’ll learn

  • The Fed does not set mortgage rates directly. Austin says the Fed moves short-term rates, while mortgage rates follow the mortgage bond market, and inflation is the biggest driver. (09:24)
  • A new Fed chair means a new way of communicating. Austin expects fewer announcements under Kevin Warsh, which could mean bigger moves when the Fed does speak. Prepare buyers for that. (10:46)
  • Investors are everyday buyers. Austin says one in three buyers is buying a rental property, and large Wall Street players are a small share of the market. (14:16)
  • DSCR loans qualify the property, not the borrower’s income. The lender looks at the rental income against the mortgage payment, which skips the job and income verification of a conventional loan. (16:38)
  • BiggerPockets is a lead source. Austin says keyword alerts for your market and local meetups have led to 10 to 15 closed transactions over the past year or so. (21:51)
  • Talk about depreciation, not just rental income. Austin’s example is a $300,000 property producing about an $8,000 yearly loss on paper over 27 and a half years. (32:05)
  • Use buydowns when rates worry buyers. A seller credit can fund a 1-0 buydown, and if a bigger ask gets a counter, a smaller concession still helps. (42:52)

“You don’t have to go big, or if you do go big, and you can’t get it, you get a counter, you can always pivot, take a smaller concession, and do a 1-0 buy down.”

Austin Clarence (at 45:05)

  • Give it time. Her YouTube channel took about a year before it really got rolling. (39:14)
  • Add local news to your content. A new store or coffee shop opening gives you a reason to make a video for the people who live there. (39:27)

“I think a lot of things take a little longer. Like for, I mean, for my YouTube channel, for instance, it took me like a solid year before I really like got rolling.”

episodes.full_description:
Watch this episode on YouTube.

In this Inner Game of Real Estate Success episode, high-performance hypnotherapist and mindset coach Paul Salter explains the “grinder identity”: the habit of outworking everyone until busyness becomes a way to avoid the harder work of growing. He covers why more effort stops paying off, how it shows up in an agent’s day, and what to do about it.

What you’ll learn

  • Your brain prefers the familiar. Paul says the nervous system favors what it knows, even when that is stress, which is why a new level of success can feel uncomfortable. (05:17)
  • Hustle alone will not get you to the next level. Paul’s message is that you cannot grind your way there. (06:13)
  • Busyness is not progress. You can be moving nonstop, taking meetings and putting out fires, and still mistake motion for progress. (10:18)
  • There is a season to grind. Early in a career, intense effort builds skill and discipline, but it becomes counterproductive when it is the only gear you have. (11:52)
  • Strengths can hide the problem. Paul gives examples such as staying in the doing instead of leading the team, and calls it sophisticated avoidance. (17:11)
  • The next level asks for different skills. It requires calm clarity and delegation, not more proving yourself. (21:23)

“You’ve become a prisoner of the identity that once saved you.”

In this Video Boot Camp for Real Estate Professionals segment, video coach Kim Rittberg gives agents a short briefing on what to do right now: why short-form video still matters most on social media, how to use AI for ideas, scripts and editing, and how to make your profile and content easy to find.

What you’ll learn

  • Short-form video is still the biggest thing on social. Kim says video gets more attention and engagement, so use more of it. (03:34)
  • Cut one home tour into several pieces. A shorter, vertical version of a home tour does well across almost all platforms, and stories work too. (03:53)
  • Use AI for ideas, scripts and editing. It can build a content calendar and write scripts from your topics, but you should edit them so they sound like you. Kim does not recommend avatar faces over a real agent on camera. (04:58)
  • Start with your clients’ biggest questions. Share what you notice in your area and read the market reports for your clients. (06:05)
  • Make yourself searchable. Social platforms act as search tools, so put your area and credibility markers in your bio. (06:38)
  • Show yourself, not just the house. Kim’s “two C’s” are connection and credibility, which keep you top of mind. (08:45)

“The important thing to know about video is it’s still the biggest thing on social media. It gets more attention, more eyes, more engagement. So if you’re not using video, use it. If you are using video, use more of it.”

  • Get the buyer agreement signed and document the hard conversations. Danny lost a $30 million buyer by not having paperwork in place, and a later dispute taught him to confirm key advice in writing. (23:37)
  • Stay lean if it fits you. Danny runs a small operation instead of a large team and says he is as profitable as agents with much bigger teams. (32:31)
  • Move up market one tier at a time. He started at lower price points, became the condo specialist in his area, and traded up with those clients over the years. He also says to learn the inventory and work open houses for productive agents. (37:16)
  • Lean into the hard part. For Danny that means making the uncomfortable call now instead of putting it off. (42:57)

  • Empathy and a clear plan won the deal. The buyers moved forward at a strong price with no concessions and told her she had spoken in a human way. (18:28)

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

In this Learning With A Lender episode, D.J. Paris talks with Austin Clarence, a mortgage loan officer and investor financing specialist with Nexa Mortgage. They cover the new Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac condo reserve rule, how bridge loans and HELOCs let buyers tap equity before a sale, and what agents can tell buyers about rates and a 2-1 buydown.

What you’ll learn

  • Condo reserve requirements are going up. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are raising the share of an HOA’s annual budget that must go to reserves from 10% to 15% for conventional loans, effective January 2027. (06:07)
  • Expect higher HOA fees. Austin says many associations sit near the old minimum and will need to raise fees to stay eligible for conventional financing. (09:22)
  • Use it to start conversations. D.J. and Austin suggest agents tell condo owners about the change and offer to speak to their HOA board. (10:02)
  • A full condo review is coming for everyone. After August 3rd, anyone buying a condo with conventional financing goes through the full review, regardless of down payment. (10:25)
  • Bridge loans let buyers skip the sale contingency. A buyer who owns a home can tap its equity for a down payment before it sells, which can make an offer stronger. (17:06)
  • HELOCs can fund a down payment. Austin explains how newer HELOC programs use automated valuations and soft credit checks, and says some close within days. (22:59)
  • A 2-1 buydown is a tool when rates are high. Austin explains how a seller-paid temporary buydown lowers the payment in the early years of the loan. (31:51)

“So bridge loans are huge because you can tap into that equity typically up to 75% of that property’s value.”

Austin Clarence (at 17:19)

  • Skip the pitch on the first call. Sarah thanks the lead for calling and sets up a consultation on Zoom or Google Meet. (07:38)

  • Treat an exploratory trip as a good sign. A buyer who wants to visit before house hunting is serious. (10:29)
  • Keep following up. Sarah says a YouTube lead who goes quiet is still a lead, so follow up with value instead of leaving them on a drip campaign. (11:49)

In the first episode of The YouTube Lab, Sarah Maslowski, a full-time agent in the Metro Atlanta area, explains how she closed $28 million in volume last year from clients who all came from YouTube. She covers which videos bring in warm leads, how to handle those leads, how often to post and what equipment you actually need.

  • Make videos about the move, not about you. Videos for people deciding whether to relocate, built around questions they already search, work better than listing videos or local business spotlights. (07:44)
  • Start with the pros and cons of your area. Be honest about traffic, taxes, schools and commute times, then add cost of living videos with real numbers and neighborhood driving tours. (10:25)
  • Keep the call to action low pressure. Sarah skips relocation guides and simply tells viewers how to reach her below the video, so the people who call are serious. (15:41)
  • Post one long video a week. Long form means at least eight minutes, with 10 to 12 minutes the sweet spot. Many agents batch two videos at a time. (19:02)
  • You only need an iPhone, a basic mic and good light. Expect it to be slow at first, and judge the first three to four months by whether people reach out, not by views. (23:57)

“YouTube rewards consistency, not intensity.”

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

D.J. Paris talks with Amanda Pendleton, Zillow’s home trends expert, about what Zillow’s survey data says buyers and sellers want from their agent in 2026. They cover why past clients don’t always come back, how buyers now find agents online, how to work with Gen Z buyers, and what today’s sellers expect.

What you’ll learn

  • Repeat buyers are the majority. Repeat buyers now make up 55% of all buyers, and they are not necessarily going back to the agent who helped them last time. (06:56)
  • Happy clients still go elsewhere. 79% of past clients say they would hire their agent again, but only 13% of repeat buyers actually do. Amanda says homeowners typically wait about 14 years to sell again, and their lives change in that time. (08:39)
  • Stay in touch in a personal way. Check in on milestones, stay visible online and talk about more than real estate, so you stay top of mind as a trusted advisor. (11:45)
  • Your online presence is part of the hire. More than a third of buyers and sellers say they found their agent online, a share that has doubled in seven years. (18:08)
  • Social media helps. 44% of prospective buyers say they are more willing to hire an agent with a social media presence. (19:52)
  • Text Gen Z buyers. If a Gen Z client texts, text back instead of calling. Amanda also notes that 46% of Gen Z buyers get a gift or loan from family or friends, compared with 35% of all buyers. (25:04)
  • Sellers are pragmatic. Amanda says more than half of sellers name maximizing price as their top priority. (33:20)

“…for an agent, this really means loyalty cannot be assumed, right.”

Amanda Pendleton (at 11:06)

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

D.J. Paris sits down with Tim Burrell, a Raleigh, North Carolina agent with RE/MAX United who is also an attorney and general contractor with 45 years of experience, and the author of The AI Negotiator. They cover how to use AI before and during a negotiation, how to build rapport with the other side, and how to keep AI honest.

What you’ll learn

  • Research the other person first. Tim runs a “super prompt” before talking with almost anyone to find their background and what the two of you have in common, then opens with that. (12:56)
  • Negotiate beyond price. Look for something that costs you little and the other side values highly, and trade it for something in return. (17:27)
  • Find out what cards they hold. Use AI to research the house and the other party’s situation, such as financial pressure or a need to close fast. (21:40)
  • Test your offer before you send it. Give AI both sides’ situations and your offer, and ask for the most probable response. (35:49)
  • Check its work and ask for honesty. AI makes mistakes, so double check it, and tell it to skip the flattery and give you unvarnished facts. (30:09)

“Instead, find out something which you’ve got in common. Establish some sort of rapport, get some kind of relationship going and then work on solving the problem.”

D.J. Paris talks with Courtney Poulos, founder and broker-owner of Acme Real Estate, a boutique brokerage in Los Angeles. Courtney is also known for her writing and her reviews of AI tools for agents. They cover her path into real estate, her renovation resale niche, how she thinks about client experience and open houses, what AI can and cannot do, and where she sees industry policy heading.

What you’ll learn

  • Persistence landed her first Los Angeles client. Courtney called a local home flipper over and over and built a spreadsheet of his acquisition and sales costs, and he finally gave her a meeting. (13:45)
  • A clear niche builds a brand. Her brokerage works with designers and flippers to reinvent homes in a more editorial way, which is the renovation resale niche she is known for. (15:00)

In this Inner Game of Real Estate Success episode, Paul Salter, a mindset and performance coach and credentialed hypnotherapist, asks whether work-life balance is the right goal for high-performing agents. He explains what chronic stress does to the brain and why he points agents toward alignment, honest communication and clarity about what they want.

What you’ll learn

  • Balance and burnout have a cost. Paul says he spent much of his career working at least 70-hour weeks, believing more was better, and that it cost him dearly. (04:35)
  • Chronic stress dulls the systems that made you elite. He explains that the part of the brain responsible for focus, creativity and decision making begins to go offline while stress hormones flood the body. (09:28)
  • Breakthroughs start with honest communication. That starts with being honest with yourself about what you want, then telling the people in your life. (18:33)
  • Aligned action beats more effort. Once you are clear on what you want, Paul says you can reverse engineer it and take action that fits. (22:49)
  • Find out what you want with a simple exercise. Three times a day, write down your answer to “what do I want?” and look for patterns. (25:08)

“Balance is not what you seek. Alignment is the answer. Alignment allows you to achieve significant and sustainable results.”

Kim Rittberg, a real estate video coach and former TV producer who has worked at Netflix and Us Weekly, explains how to become the go-to agent in your town. She focuses on credibility and the kinds of video that build it, whether an agent is brand new or has been working for 20 years.

  • New agents can show a day in the life. Footage of homes that aren’t your listings works too, and so do market updates. (08:50)
  • Don’t give viewers homework. Skip the chart in a market update. Give people the three most important facts in plain English. (09:28)

Paul Salter, a mindset and performance coach who uses hypnosis, hosts this monthly Inner Game of Real Estate Success episode on keeping your self-worth separate from your results. He explains why attachment to outcomes is a learned pattern, what it costs agents and their teams, and how to shift your focus to your process.

  • Attachment to results is learned. Paul traces it to childhood, when praise followed wins and grades, and says that what was learned can be unlearned. (05:09)
  • Clinging to an outcome can push it away. Paul describes an agent with 11 years in the business who treated every deal as a verdict on his worth, and who started rushing and forcing offers. (09:24)

  • Measure the process, not just the scoreboard. If you can say you executed your process with integrity and energy, Paul calls that a win. (18:35)
  • Results lag effort. Cast as many lines in the water as you can, and expect the bite to come in a week, a month or a year. (21:55)

“Your attachment to results is a collection of learned beliefs, feelings and behaviors. It can be unlearned.”

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

D.J. Paris talks with Jeremy Hurewitz, a former foreign correspondent who now works in corporate security and wrote the book Sell Like a Spy. They cover what spies and agents have in common, including understanding motivation, mirroring, reading body language and asking fewer questions, and how to use those skills with buyers and sellers.

What you’ll learn

  • Start with what motivates the person. Jeremy says spies do not try to change someone’s mind. They work to understand what drives the person across the table. (11:54)
  • Mirror subtly. Practice with friends and family, start small, and do not lose yourself. Matching someone’s pet phrases, posture and expressions builds comfort quickly. (16:04)
  • Read the room. If the list price comes up and someone rubs the back of their neck, that is a soothing gesture. Folded arms or an object placed between you can be a blocking gesture. Look for a pattern before you conclude anything. (18:16)
  • Let upset clients vent. Do not interrupt or correct. Then invite them to help solve the problem. (23:19)
  • Elicit instead of interrogating. Make an open statement or share something about yourself and let the other person fill in the details. Jeremy says peppering people with questions makes them feel interrogated. (42:17)
  • Take notes right after you meet. Do a brain dump as soon as you leave a client so you do not misremember what they told you. (43:42)

“…spies are the world’s best salespeople because there is no harder sale to make.”

Jeremy Hurewitz (at 09:43)

  • Connect across differences. Dan’s steps are to build rapport, ask deep questions and listen to the person’s energy, then find the commonalities. (45:22)

“Sales is about leading. And if you’re struggling in sales, you’re probably doing it wrong.”

episodes.full_description:

D.J. Paris talks with Lauren Duke, founder and CEO of CoreOps Collective and the former COO of a top 10 mega real estate team. They cover how to decide when to build a team, how to run a time audit, what to look for in a hire, and the five systems every agent needs to scale.

What you’ll learn

  • Build a business that does not depend on you. Lauren says the best advice she got came from a book called Clockwork, and that controlling every part of the business makes it close to impossible to grow. (04:33)
  • Know what you want from life first. Lauren says you cannot decide when to hire without knowing how many hours you want to work and what your family life should look like. (14:56)
  • Run a time audit. Write down how you actually spend your week, as you would a food diary, and have someone else look at it. (19:03)
  • Six hours of lead generation with no leads is a conversion problem. Lauren says that is a skills issue, not a time issue. (21:36)
  • A team is more than other agents. A transaction coordinator, a trusted attorney, a title company or a financial advisor can be part of your team. (24:11)
  • Hire for culture fit first. Skill can be taught, and anyone who joins your business is an extension of you. (27:04)
  • Connect your five pillars. Lauren names lead generation and marketing, operations, financials, client experience and team, and says the piece most agents are missing is the integration of all five. (31:47)

“…if you have a business that depends on you, you don’t have a business, you have a job. And your boss is a psychopath.”

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

In this Learn With A Lender episode, D.J. Paris talks with Christian Bachelder, co-founder of The One Brokerage and a licensed mortgage broker who invests in short-term rentals. They cover why mortgage rates had dropped ahead of an expected Fed cut, how builder incentives work, and how real estate investors use depreciation and the tax code.

What you’ll learn

  • Mortgage rates move on expectations. Christian says lenders price ahead of what the Fed is expected to do, and that a September quarter-point cut was already built into pricing. (06:07)
  • Rates had fallen from about seven percent. At the time of recording, Christian says a primary residence could realistically get a rate between 6.2 and 6.5. (08:33)
  • Know who else wants the same property. A buyer who targets a property that also suits a flipper or investor is competing with them, so widening the search to the suburbs or to a duplex can improve the odds of an accepted offer. (11:22)
  • Builder credits protect the sales price. Christian says a closing cost credit keeps a builder from lowering the price on every other home in the development, and that builder funds can buy a rate down. (15:28)
  • Depreciation is the investor’s tax tool. Christian says his biggest motivation for investing is the tax benefits, and describes a cabin in the Smoky Mountains that gave him a $350,000 tax write off. (23:13)
  • Short-term rentals reward good operators. Christian does not think the market is over-saturated, and says it is under-saturated with good properties. (25:49)
  • Talk to someone who has done it. Before buying your first investment property, Christian recommends talking to an operator, property managers and an investor-minded agent. (30:07)

“And if I can put $100,000 into the down payment of a property instead of sending it to the IRS, I’m gonna do that every time.”

D.J. Paris sits down with Sarah Maslowski, a top 1% agent in North Metro Atlanta and YouTube content creator. She shares how she went from teaching to real estate, and how weekly YouTube videos for people moving to her area became her main source of leads.

  • Old videos keep working. YouTube can suggest a video you made two years ago to someone who has never seen it. (30:18)

“And the cool thing about YouTube videos is that you don’t need a ton of views on your videos. You just need the right people to watch your videos.”

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

D.J. Paris sits down with Lou Adler, co-founder and principal of Real New York, a midsize full-service brokerage in New York City. They cover how Lou built the firm by working with developers and landlords, how he gives new agents real opportunities, and why he puts the relationship ahead of the commission.

What you’ll learn

  • Keep reinventing the business. After New York’s rent law changes, Lou says the firm survived by growing new arms like commercial, sales and rentals instead of staying the course. (05:48)
  • Hire when opportunities outgrow you. Real New York started organically and hired another agent each time it had more opportunities than it could handle. (31:21)
  • Control the inventory. D.J. and Lou discuss why agents who build relationships with landlords and developers hold the listings, instead of only finding a place for one client. (36:14)
  • Screening tenants has changed. Lou says the firm now uses biometric screening because of AI, after seeing fake employment letters, pay stubs and bank statements. (38:37)
  • Put the relationship first. Lou says the firm has always put its client’s commission last and the relationship first. (44:23)

“We’ve always put their commission last, we’ve always put the relationship first, you know, whatever we need to do to make sure that we are transacting for this developer or landlord this client we will do.”

episodes.full_description:

In this month’s Better Your Business With Ben, D.J. Paris talks with Ben Lalez of Compass and David Fields, sales director of the Ben Lalez Team in the Chicago area. They ask whether AI could take over a whole transaction, where agents still add value, and how their team uses AI today.

What you’ll learn

  • AI may start doing the work, not just answering. Ben pictures AI tools that search listings, schedule showings, suggest an offer price and line up inspections within a few years. (03:50)
  • Guiding people through a stressful purchase is the agent’s edge. Ben’s argument is that the agent handles the emotional side while AI handles facts, figures and operations. (08:19)
  • AI can tell you what you want to hear. Ben describes an AI tool that said it could do a task, then admitted it couldn’t, and said it wanted to please him. Check its work. (16:57)
  • Build your own AI advantage. The team talks about custom GPTs and language models trained on your own data as a unique value proposition. (19:23)
  • Use ChatGPT for training. David describes role-playing a room of agents against an AI that gives hard objections for 45 minutes. (29:20)

“…I still think that there’s inherent value to the human being, the relationships, the trust that you build.”

Ben Lalez (at 18:20)

D.J. Paris sits down with Ryan Bruen, team lead of the Bruen Team serving Morris and Somerset counties in New Jersey. Ryan covers what is holding buyers and sellers back, how smart home technology fits into his business, and the habits he uses to stay close to past clients.

  • Treat a primary home as a lifestyle choice. Ryan says people should not look at their primary home as an investment, and that the best reasons to own are not financial. (22:38)

  • Work on the business when it’s slow. Ryan uses slower periods to improve his systems and plan ahead. (56:19)

“I’d say a lot of agents seem to focus a lot on new lead generation. I focus a lot more of my energy on client relationship management.”

In this Monday Market Minute, D.J. Paris sits down with Carrie McCormick of the Carrie McCormick Real Estate Group with @properties Christie’s International Real Estate in Chicago. episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

In this month’s Learn With A Lender, D.J. Paris talks with Christian Bachelder, co-founder of The One Brokerage and a licensed real estate agent, insurance and mortgage broker. They cover what to tell clients who don’t want to give up a low mortgage rate, then turn to where rates may be headed and the return of 100% bonus depreciation.

What you’ll learn

  • Home equity is not locked. A HELOC or a second mortgage lets an owner tap equity and keep a low first-mortgage rate. (06:57)
  • Consider keeping the house as a rental. Christian says that with a rate around 2.5% or 3%, a rented property will likely cash flow in most markets. (09:00)
  • A low rate is cheap money. If your rate is at or below inflation, you are borrowing money for free in effect. (11:43)
  • Selling and renting can be fine. If you can’t convert the property to a rental, selling, renting for a while and taking your winnings off the table is not a terrible idea. (14:22)
  • Bonus depreciation is back. Christian explains how front-loading depreciation can offset income, and says he took about a 00,000 write-off on a .6 million property. (24:25)

“…just strictly speaking from like the best financial advice I could give, being a landlord is worth saving your 2% rate.”

Christian Bachelder (at 10:04)

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

D.J. Paris talks with Kamryn Reynolds of Articulate Advantage, a coaching firm that helps professionals master their voice, about simple changes that improve how agents communicate. They cover authenticity, how to ask for referrals, mirroring a client’s words, and why tone of voice matters as much as the words.

What you’ll learn

  • Authenticity can’t be faked. People sense when someone is holding something back, so connection starts with being genuine. (17:36)
  • Get curious about what lights people up. Asking about a passion or hobby beats small talk about the weather. (24:02)
  • Make referrals specific. Tell people exactly who a good referral is and how to connect you, instead of a vague “send me anyone.” (35:43)
  • Mirror and label. Repeat the last words a client says, and use labels that start with “It sounds like…” so they feel heard. (42:19)
  • Watch your tone. Ending sentences on an uptick makes statements sound like questions, so keep your intonation flat or downward. (48:16)

“…however good you are at your job, however intelligent, however smart you are, people perceive you at the level of your communication, not at the level of your capability.”

Kamryn Reynolds (at 20:53)

Real estate video coach Kim Rittberg interviews Sabina Hichen, a small business media strategist known as the PR Fairy Godmother and the founder of Press for Success. They cover why agents should go after press coverage, how to start with local outlets, and three kinds of stories agents can pitch.

What you’ll learn

  • Press builds visibility, differentiation and authority. Seeing an agent on a local morning show or reading their advice online helps a client choose them. (05:39)
  • Start local. Find where real estate stories already run in your local paper, TV station and websites, and get to know the reporters there. (11:39)
  • Pitch expert tips. Seasonal, evergreen advice, such as how to stage a home, is the first type of story Sabina recommends. (15:26)
  • Piggyback on hot topics. Respond to news, surveys and studies by translating them for local buyers and sellers. (20:24)
  • Tell your founder story. Agents are entrepreneurs, so weave in your own story. It can be an everyday moment and not a dramatic one. (21:54)

“But if you learn how to convert your content into cash, that is the key to growing as an agent in the modern era where social media is so important.”

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

In this Learn With A Lender episode, D.J. Paris talks with Christian Bachelder, co-founder of The One Brokerage, about whether mortgage rates are too high to buy right now. Christian explains what agents can say to buyers, how to use price negotiation and rate buydowns, when refinancing makes sense, and how he picks investment markets.

What you’ll learn

  • Every market has a way to respond. Whatever rates or the Fed are doing, Christian says there is a strategy to combat it. (09:47)
  • Negotiate the purchase price. With less competition than in recent years, buyers have more power on price, even as they worry about the rate. (10:01)
  • Consider a temporary buydown. Christian walks through a 2-1 buydown, which lowers the rate for the first years of the loan. (10:28)
  • Refinance when the savings are real. His general guidance is to look at it once you can save around 1% on your rate. (12:44)
  • Look for population growth in investment markets. Christian calls it a common-sense approach to look at what thousands of new people moving to an area will do to demand. (23:42)

“What I’m getting at is every single market, every response of interest rates or the Fed or whatever’s happening has a way to combat it.”

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

In this live webinar, D.J. Paris hosts Mary-Lou Dingman, a real estate coach with The Locker Room and a 22-year industry veteran from North Carolina. She walks through the top 10 mistakes agents make at open houses and the system she uses to turn each one into appointments, from inviting neighbors to following up the same week.

What you’ll learn

  • You don’t need your own listing. Mary-Lou says to find the listings and agents in the areas you want, set up a search that comes to you, and offer to hold their open houses. (11:47)
  • Add virtual open houses. She describes an agent she coached who ran three virtual open houses between Christmas and New Year’s and picked up buyer and seller clients from them. (15:16)
  • Ask for the appointment while they’re in the house. Tell visitors up front you’ll meet them in the kitchen to hear their feedback and set a time to see if you’re a good fit. (19:17)
  • Do the math on one appointment per open house. Four open houses a month for ten months is 40 appointments. (20:39)
  • Invite the neighbors. Invite at least 25 neighbors, door knock when you put your signs out, and offer a sneak peek before the open house. (16:22)

“There are people that I am meant to help. And all I have to do is my part to find them.”

Mary-Lou Dingman (at 18:24)

episodes.full_description:
Watch this interview on YouTube.

In this Learn With A Lender episode, D.J. Paris talks with Christian Bachelder, cofounder of The One Brokerage. Christian sorts mortgage products into buckets by how they are underwritten, then explains bank statement loans, investor loans and hard money, and walks through a deal of his own that used several of them.

What you’ll learn

  • Think of lending in three buckets. Christian splits loans by how they are underwritten, from strict criteria and the best terms down to the loosest criteria and the highest cost. (07:26)
  • Investor loans can qualify on the property. In the investor-friendly bucket the question is whether the property cash flows, not what is on your tax returns. (11:13)
  • Bank statement loans suit self-employed buyers. A lender looks at roughly the last 12 months of bank statements instead of what ends up on the tax returns. (14:17)
  • Hard money can bridge a rehab. In his own deal, a hard money loan financed 90% of the project cost, and he refinanced into a 30-year loan afterward. (20:01)
  • Commercial is a fourth bucket. Apartment complexes, warehouses and similar properties sit in a separate commercial category. (24:01)

“You don’t need tax returns. You don’t need all the mess of documentation. Basically, we’re saying if it makes dollars, it makes sense kind of thing.”

Christian Bachelder (at 11:18)
